title: Avoiding wrong-address delivery orders
description: Avoid wrong-address delivery order mistakes with a simple phone script, address check steps, and a cleaner delivery workflow.
question: How do I avoid wrong-address delivery orders at my restaurant?
answer: Use a short address-check script on every delivery call, repeat the street number and apartment or suite back to the caller, and confirm the phone number before sending the ticket. Keep your menu and address details current on your phone host so the caller hears the right pickup or delivery info before the order is finished.
summary: You’ll learn a simple phone process that cuts down on wrong-address delivery orders.
intro:
A wrong-address delivery order usually starts with a rushed call and one missing detail. The fix is to confirm the full address the same way every time, then repeat it back before you send the ticket.

For busy pizza shops, takeout spots, delis, and family restaurants, that means a short script, a clear ticket, and a calm handoff when the address is unclear. ROAL can help here because it answers the phone, takes the order, and confirms the caller’s details from the restaurant’s live menu and info.

sections.h2: Why do wrong-address delivery orders happen?
sections.body:
Most wrong-address delivery orders come from simple phone-call mistakes, not bad intent. The caller may give a street name but forget the apartment number, say the wrong town, or assume the driver knows the area.

A delivery order should be treated like a checklist, not a conversation that gets loosely remembered. Here’s a basic flow you can train your team on:

1. Get the full delivery address first.
2. Repeat the street number, street name, apartment or suite, city, and ZIP.
3. Confirm the best callback number.
4. Repeat the order and the ready time.
5. Send the ticket only after the caller says yes.

A simple phone line helps: "Before I place that, can I confirm the full delivery address, including apartment or suite number?" That one sentence catches a lot of mistakes before the food leaves the kitchen.

sections.h2: What should you ask on every delivery call?
sections.body:
You do not need a long script. You need the same few questions every time so no one skips the important parts during a rush.

Use this order when taking a delivery call:

- Name
- Callback phone number
- Full delivery address
- Apartment, floor, unit, or suite number
- City and ZIP
- Order items and modifiers
- Ready time

A good script line is: "Just to make sure the driver gets there cleanly, can you repeat the street number and apartment number for me?" That helps when a caller says, for example, "123 Main" but actually lives in Apt. 4B. If your delivery area includes nearby towns, ask the town name too. Many wrong-address problems come from crossing city lines without noticing.

If you use ROAL, it can collect the caller’s name and phone, repeat the order back, and send a clean ticket to the kitchen screen. It also answers questions about address, hours, parking, and the menu, so fewer calls get rushed or half-finished.

sections.h2: How do you confirm the address before the food leaves?
sections.body:
The best place to catch a wrong address is before the ticket hits the kitchen screen. That way, the cook is not making food for an address you cannot serve.

Use this quick confirmation checklist before you mark the order complete:

| Checkpoint | What to say | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Street address | "Can you confirm the full street number and name?" | Stops house-number mix-ups |
| Unit info | "Do you have an apartment, suite, or floor number?" | Prevents missed drop-offs in buildings |
| City | "Which city should I put on the ticket?" | Catches wrong-town errors |
| Phone number | "What’s the best number to reach you if the driver needs help?" | Gives the driver a backup contact |
| Order recap | "So I have [items], to [address], ready at [time]. Is that correct?" | Gives one last chance to fix it |

A worked example: say the caller orders a $28 lunch combo and gives you "55 Oak Street, second floor." Plug in your own order value, then ask one more question: "Is that second floor or Unit 2?" That tiny check can save you from a wasted delivery and a remake.

sections.h2: How can your menu and hours reduce address confusion?
sections.body:
Wrong-address delivery orders are often part of a bigger problem: the caller is not getting the right basic info from the first person or system that answers. If your hours, delivery area, or address are outdated, people guess.

Keep these items current everywhere the phone host reads from:

- Restaurant name
- Full address
- Delivery area rules
- Hours
- Menu items and prices
- Sold-out items

A clear phone response sounds like this: "We deliver to that area during dinner hours only, and I can confirm the address before I place the order." That tells the caller exactly what to do next.

ROAL reads menu, prices, hours, and address from public pages or an uploaded menu. That matters because the host can answer common questions without passing callers around. If a caller asks for the address or hours, the answer should be the same every time. For more setup context, see [How it works](/how-it-works) and [Questions owners ask](/faq).

sections.h2: What should you do when the address still feels unclear?
sections.body:
Sometimes the caller is confused, the building is hard to find, or the address sounds incomplete. In that case, do not guess. Pause and ask for one more detail.

Use a simple escalation rule:

1. Ask for the nearest cross street.
2. Ask for the building name or landmark.
3. Ask for the unit, buzzer, or gate code if your staff already collects those details.
4. If it still sounds unclear, hand it to staff with a short summary.

A useful line is: "I want to make sure the driver gets to the right place, so let me get one more detail from you." That is friendly and direct.

ROAL can hand tricky calls to staff with a summary when it cannot answer safely. That is important for allergy-sensitive questions, manager requests, catering, and any call where the address or instructions are too messy to trust to memory. The point is not to force automation. The point is to protect the order and keep the kitchen from making food for the wrong drop-off.

sections.h2: How do phone setup and forwarding help busy teams?
sections.body:
A lot of wrong-address delivery orders happen when the phone rings during a rush and someone answers too fast. When the line is busy or unanswered, calls can go to voicemail or get rushed by a stressed team member.

If you want a cleaner setup, forward your restaurant’s existing number to a phone host during busy times or for all calls, depending on how you run the shop. On many carriers and systems, forwarding can be set with carrier codes or in a business phone portal, but codes vary. Always confirm with your carrier and test with a call.

For a general reference, [call forwarding codes by carrier](/tools/call-forwarding-codes) can help you compare common options, and [short-staffed shifts](/use-cases/short-staffed) explains why restaurants often use forwarding during peak hours. ROAL gives each location its own phone line automatically once the owner claims the host, and forwarding can be turned off any time. That means you keep your number and control when the host picks up.

sections.h2: What should you do this week to cut wrong-address orders?
sections.body:
You do not need a big project. You need a repeatable habit your team can use on the next shift.

Try this 5-step action plan:

1. Write a one-line address check script.
2. Put the full address and delivery area in your phone notes and public pages.
3. Train the counter person or phone host to repeat the address back.
4. Add one extra question for apartments, suites, and floor numbers.
5. Review one day of call history and see where the mistakes started.

If you want a phone host that can answer the phone, take the order, confirm the caller’s details, and send a clean ticket to the kitchen screen, you can [build a free test host from your website](/try). ROAL is pre-launch, so keep expectations practical: it does not take card numbers over the phone, and tricky calls still go to staff.

A lot of owners compare phone orders with delivery apps because delivery apps often take a large commission per order, while ROAL charges per completed phone order. For a rough pricing comparison, see [Pay per order vs monthly AI phone plans](/compare/monthly-ai-phone-plans) and [Pricing](/pricing).

takeaways: Always confirm street number, unit, city, and callback number before sending a delivery ticket.
Use the same short address script on every call so no one skips a step during rush.
Keep your hours, address, and delivery rules current so callers hear the right information.
Hand unclear or risky calls to staff with a summary instead of guessing.
A clean ticket and a repeat-back reduce mix-ups between the phone and the kitchen.

faq.q: What causes wrong-address delivery orders most often?
faq.a: Usually it is a missed apartment number, the wrong city, or a caller giving an incomplete address while everyone is rushed. The best fix is a consistent confirmation script that repeats the full address back before the order is sent to the kitchen.

faq.q: Should I ask for apartment or suite numbers every time?
faq.a: Yes, if you deliver to buildings, offices, or multi-unit homes. Ask for the unit number even if the caller seems sure you already have it, because that is one of the most common places mistakes happen.

faq.q: Can an AI phone host help with address checking?
faq.a: Yes. ROAL can answer the phone, take the order, collect the caller’s name and phone, and confirm the order back before sending a clean ticket to the kitchen screen. If the address is unclear or the call is sensitive, it can hand the conversation to staff with a summary.

faq.q: What should I say when I need to double-check an address without sounding rude?
faq.a: Say, "I want to make sure the driver gets there cleanly, so can you repeat the full address for me?" That keeps the tone friendly and makes the check feel normal, not suspicious.
